definition: A specific statement of what the intern intends to be able to do by the end of the placement.
wrongs: A vague wish to have a good experience, with no ability named.
The employer's profit target for the quarter.
The number of hours in a working week.
why: A learning objective names a capability the intern should gain, so progress can be judged.
example: By week ten the intern aims to configure a basic network switch using the team's checklist.
scenario: The placement plan says have a good time and names no capability. Which replacement is a learning objective?
scenarioAnswer: Be able to configure a switch using the team checklist by week ten
scenarioWrongs: Have a good experience
Help the firm raise quarterly profit
Work thirty-five hours each week
scenarioWhy: A learning objective states a specific ability the intern should have by a stated point.

definition: A written plan, agreed by the intern, workplace, and university, that sets goals, duties, and supervision.
wrongs: A secret note the intern writes and never shows to the supervisor.
The company's annual financial statement.
A bus timetable for the commute.
why: A learning agreement is the shared plan of goals, duties, and supervision among intern, host, and university.
example: The intern, workplace supervisor, and tutor sign a plan listing duties, weekly meetings, and two learning goals.
scenario: Goals and weekly supervision must be agreed by you, the host, and the university before the placement. Which document records that?
scenarioAnswer: The learning agreement
scenarioWrongs: A private note nobody else sees
The company's financial statement
The bus timetable
scenarioWhy: The learning agreement is the shared written plan of goals, duties, and supervision.

definition: The staff member at the host organisation who assigns the intern's work and gives day-to-day feedback.
wrongs: The university tutor who never visits the workplace and does not assign daily tasks.
A friend who texts advice but has no role at the host.
The receptionist who issues a visitor badge only.
why: The workplace supervisor is the host employee responsible for assigning work and supervising it.
example: Each morning the network engineer assigns the intern a ticket and reviews the result that afternoon.
scenario: Someone at the host must assign today's ticket and review it later. Which role is that?
scenarioAnswer: The workplace supervisor
scenarioWrongs: The university tutor who is not on site
A friend with no role at the host
The receptionist who only issues badges
scenarioWhy: The workplace supervisor assigns host work and reviews it during the placement.

definition: The university staff member who checks the placement against academic requirements and assesses the intern's learning.
wrongs: The host employee who assigns daily operational tasks.
A classmate on a different placement.
The client whose product the intern is testing.
why: The academic supervisor represents the university's learning and assessment requirements.
example: The tutor reads the mid-placement report and checks that the work still matches the approved learning goals.
scenario: The mid-placement report must be judged against university learning goals. Which person is responsible for that academic check?
scenarioAnswer: The academic supervisor
scenarioWrongs: The host employee who assigns tickets
A classmate on another placement
The external client
scenarioWhy: The academic supervisor monitors and assesses the placement against university requirements.

definition: A scheduled conversation in which the intern and supervisor review progress, problems, and the next tasks.
wrongs: A silent desk session with no review of work.
The fire-alarm drill for the whole building.
A social lunch with no discussion of tasks.
why: A supervision meeting is planned time to review progress and set the next work.
example: Every Thursday the intern and supervisor spend thirty minutes on finished tickets, blockers, and next week's tasks.
scenario: You need a set time to review blockers and agree next week's tasks with your supervisor. Which event is that?
scenarioAnswer: A supervision meeting
scenarioWrongs: A silent desk session
The building fire drill
A social lunch with no work discussed
scenarioWhy: A supervision meeting is the scheduled review of progress, problems, and upcoming tasks.

definition: The behaviour expected at work, including punctuality, respect, honesty, and following local rules.
wrongs: Behaving exactly as you would at a private party, including ignoring start times.
A technical standard for cable colours.
The intern's hobby outside working hours that does not affect work.
why: Workplace conduct is the standard of behaviour the host expects while the intern is at work.
example: The intern arrives on time, speaks respectfully in client calls, and does not share passwords.
scenario: You are late without warning and joke about a client on a call. Which standard have you missed?
scenarioAnswer: Workplace conduct
scenarioWrongs: A cable-colour standard
A weekend hobby that does not affect work
The right to ignore start times as if at a party
scenarioWhy: Punctuality and respectful behaviour toward clients are part of workplace conduct.

definition: Arriving and delivering work at the agreed time, and warning the supervisor early if a delay is unavoidable.
wrongs: Arriving whenever convenient as long as the total weekly hours look similar.
Finishing early and leaving without telling anyone about unfinished shared work.
Sending an apology only after missing a client meeting.
why: Punctuality means meeting agreed times and giving early warning when a delay cannot be avoided.
example: The intern messages the supervisor at 7 a.m. that a train cancellation will make them twenty minutes late.
scenario: A cancelled train will make you late for the standup. Which action shows punctuality?
scenarioAnswer: Warn the supervisor before the meeting
scenarioWrongs: Arrive when convenient and say nothing
Apologise only after the client meeting was missed
Skip the warning because weekly hours will balance
scenarioWhy: Punctuality includes early warning when an agreed time cannot be met.

definition: Clothing and grooming that meet the host organisation's standard for the workplace and the day's duties.
wrongs: Whatever is most comfortable at home, even if the host forbids it on site.
A costume that hides a required safety vest.
A uniform from a different employer that misidentifies you.
why: Professional dress follows the host's standard and the safety needs of the day's work.
example: On a client-site day the intern wears the smart clothes named in the induction, plus the required visitor badge.
scenario: Induction says client-site days require smart clothes and a visitor badge, not gym wear. Which choice meets professional dress?
scenarioAnswer: Smart clothes and the visitor badge
scenarioWrongs: Gym wear because it is comfortable
A costume that covers the required safety vest
Another company's uniform
scenarioWhy: Professional dress follows the host's stated standard for that day's duties.

definition: The duty not to share the organisation's or clients' non-public information beyond people authorised to see it.
wrongs: A duty to post interesting client stories on a public blog for your portfolio.
Permission to discuss live incidents in a crowded cafe.
A rule that applies only to full-time staff and never to interns.
why: Interns share the duty to keep non-public organisational and client information within authorised people.
example: The intern refuses to describe a client's outage when friends ask about the placement over dinner.
scenario: Friends ask for details of a client's outage that is not public. Which response keeps workplace confidentiality?
scenarioAnswer: Decline and keep the details private
scenarioWrongs: Describe the outage for your portfolio blog
Discuss the live incident in a crowded cafe
Share it because interns are exempt
scenarioWhy: Workplace confidentiality forbids sharing non-public client information with unauthorised people.

definition: Collecting, storing, and sending client information only in the ways the workplace policy allows.
wrongs: Copying client files to a personal laptop so they are easier to read at home.
Pasting client records into a private chat because it is faster.
Leaving printed client lists on a train seat.
why: Client data must stay on approved systems and follow the host policy for collection, storage, and transfer.
example: The intern stores a client export only on the approved drive and does not email it to a personal account.
scenario: You want a client export at home tonight. Policy allows only the approved drive. Which action is correct client data handling?
scenarioAnswer: Leave the export on the approved drive
scenarioWrongs: Copy it to a personal laptop
Paste the records into a private chat
Print it and read it on the train
scenarioWhy: Client data handling means using only the storage and transfer methods the workplace policy allows.

definition: Deliberate thinking about what happened, what was learned, and what should be done differently next time.
wrongs: Copying the day's task list with no thought about learning.
Blaming others and deciding nothing will change.
Waiting until graduation and then forgetting the placement.
why: Reflection connects an experience to learning and to a change in future action.
example: After a confusing client call, the intern notes the missing question and plans to confirm the goal at the start next time.
scenario: A client call went badly because you never confirmed the goal. Which note shows reflection?
scenarioAnswer: Next time confirm the goal at the start
scenarioWrongs: A copied task list with no lesson
A note that only blames the client and changes nothing
A decision to forget the call
scenarioWhy: Reflection turns the experience into a specific change for next time.

definition: A regular written record of experiences, lessons, and next steps, kept to show learning during the placement.
wrongs: A timesheet that records only hours.
A public social post about clients.
The company's audited accounts.
why: A reflective journal is a continuing private record of experience and learning, not a timesheet or a public post.
example: Each Friday the intern writes what was tried, what failed, and one change for the following week.
scenario: The tutor wants weekly evidence of what you learned, not only hours worked. Which record fits?
scenarioAnswer: A reflective journal
scenarioWrongs: A timesheet of hours only
A public post about a client
The audited accounts
scenarioWhy: A reflective journal regularly records experiences, lessons, and next steps.

definition: A six-stage structure for reflection: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, and action plan.
wrongs: A project schedule of design, build, and test.
A statistical test of two group means.
A fire-evacuation route with six exits.
why: Gibbs' cycle is a known sequence for structured reflection ending in an action plan.
example: The intern describes a failed demo, notes feeling rushed, evaluates what worked, and ends with a plan to rehearse.
scenario: You must structure a reflection from what happened through to a next action. Which sequence matches Gibbs' cycle?
scenarioAnswer: Description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan
scenarioWrongs: Design, build, and test
Null, test, and p-value
Alarm, exit, and assembly point only
scenarioWhy: Gibbs' reflective cycle moves from description and feelings through evaluation and analysis to a conclusion and action plan.

definition: A record of hours worked, usually by day and task, submitted so attendance and effort can be verified.
wrongs: A reflective essay about feelings, with no hours.
A payslip issued by the payroll department.
A project Gantt chart for the whole company.
why: A timesheet records the hours the intern worked so the host and university can verify attendance and effort.
example: The intern enters six hours on Tuesday against network tickets and submits the sheet each Friday.
scenario: The university asks for proof of the hours you worked each day. Which record should you submit?
scenarioAnswer: A timesheet
scenarioWrongs: A feelings essay with no hours
A payslip you did not create
The company Gantt chart
scenarioWhy: A timesheet is the record of hours worked, used to verify attendance and effort.

definition: A log of days present, absent, or late, used to confirm that the placement requirement was met.
wrongs: A diary of technical lessons learned.
A list of software versions installed.
A menu of the staff canteen.
why: An attendance record shows presence and absence, which universities often require for a valid placement.
example: The sheet shows the intern present every weekday in March except one sick day notified that morning.
scenario: The faculty must confirm you were present for the required days, aside from notified absence. Which log is checked?
scenarioAnswer: The attendance record
scenarioWrongs: A journal of technical lessons
A list of installed software
The canteen menu
scenarioWhy: The attendance record logs days present, absent, or late against the placement requirement.

definition: Information from a supervisor or colleague about the quality of your work and how it can improve.
wrongs: A salary figure on a contract.
A compliment with no information about the work.
An automated out-of-office reply.
why: Feedback tells you how the work was judged and what to change; it is more than praise or a contractual number.
example: The supervisor says the network diagram was accurate but the labels were too small for the client to read.
scenario: You need to know how your diagram was judged and what to change. Which message is feedback?
scenarioAnswer: The diagram is accurate, but the labels are too small to read
scenarioWrongs: Your salary is stated in the contract
Nice work, with no further detail
An out-of-office reply
scenarioWhy: Feedback gives information about quality and a specific improvement.

definition: Specific comments that describe what worked, what did not, and what change is expected, without personal attack.
wrongs: A general insult about the person's character.
Praise that names no behaviour worth repeating.
Silence after a failed task.
why: Constructive feedback is specific and forward-looking, and it separates the work from a personal attack.
example: The supervisor says the summary missed the risk section and asks for that section in the next draft by Friday.
scenario: A draft missed the risk section. Which comment is constructive feedback?
scenarioAnswer: Add the risk section in Friday's draft
scenarioWrongs: You are careless as a person
Good job, with no detail
No comment after the failed draft
scenarioWhy: Constructive feedback names the gap and the expected change without attacking the person.

definition: Suggestions aimed at improving the next piece of work, rather than only judging work already finished.
wrongs: A final mark with no advice for the next task.
A complaint about a task that will not be repeated and with no transferable advice.
A record of hours already worked.
why: Feedforward points to the next performance so the person can apply the advice immediately.
example: Before the next client call, the supervisor advises the intern to restate the goal in the first minute.
scenario: Tomorrow's client call has not happened. The supervisor tells you to restate the goal in the first minute. Which label fits that advice?
scenarioAnswer: Feedforward
scenarioWrongs: A final mark with no advice
A complaint with no transferable point
A timesheet of past hours
scenarioWhy: Advice aimed at the next piece of work is feedforward.

definition: A work message with a clear subject, a courteous greeting, a short statement of purpose, and a professional sign-off.
wrongs: A message that starts with hey and contains only an unexplained attachment.
A chat line written in all capitals with no context.
A text to friends using nicknames and no sign-off.
why: Professional email is identifiable, polite, and purposeful so a busy reader can act on it.
example: The intern emails the supervisor with the subject Draft network diagram, a greeting, one question, and a full name.
scenario: You must ask your supervisor a question by email. Which message is professional?
scenarioAnswer: A clear subject, greeting, one question, and your full name
scenarioWrongs: Hey plus an unexplained attachment
An all-capitals chat line with no context
A nickname text with no sign-off
scenarioWhy: A professional email states the topic, is courteous, gives the purpose, and shows who sent it.

definition: The short heading of an email that states the topic so the reader can prioritise and find the message later.
wrongs: A blank heading because the body will explain everything.
The single word hello on every message you send.
A full copy of the email body pasted into the heading.
why: The subject line is a specific heading that helps the recipient sort and retrieve the message.
example: The heading Leave request 12 May is used instead of a blank subject on a message about that day.
scenario: You are requesting leave on 12 May. Which subject line helps the supervisor find the message later?
scenarioAnswer: Leave request 12 May
scenarioWrongs: A blank subject
Hello
The entire email body copied into the subject
scenarioWhy: A subject line should state the specific topic so the message can be prioritised and found.

definition: A copy of an email sent to people who should see the message but are not the primary person expected to act.
wrongs: The main recipient who is expected to carry out the request.
A hidden copy used to conceal a recipient from everyone else.
A printed photocopy of a paper letter.
why: Carbon copy informs secondary readers, while the To field holds the person expected to act.
example: The intern addresses the request to the supervisor and copies the academic tutor so the tutor can see it.
scenario: The supervisor must act, and the tutor should see the request but is not asked to act. Where should the tutor's address go?
scenarioAnswer: On carbon copy
scenarioWrongs: As the only To recipient, with the supervisor omitted
On a hidden copy so the supervisor cannot see the tutor
On a paper photocopy instead of the email
scenarioWhy: Carbon copy is for someone who should see the email but is not the primary actor.

definition: The email action that sends a response to every recipient of the original message, suitable only when all of them need it.
wrongs: A reply that goes only to the sender, which is right when others do not need it.
A new message to an unrelated department.
Deleting the original thread.
why: Reply all widens the audience to every listed recipient, so it should be used only when each person needs the response.
example: Asked a private question by one manager on a twenty-person thread, the intern replies only to that manager.
scenario: One manager asks you a private question on a twenty-person thread, and the others do not need the answer. Which action fits?
scenarioAnswer: Reply only to that manager
scenarioWrongs: Reply all with the private answer
Forward the private answer to an unrelated department
Delete the thread so nobody can read the question
scenarioWhy: Reply all is appropriate only when every recipient needs the response, which they do not here.

definition: The briefing at the start of a placement that explains site hazards, emergency routes, and the rules that keep people safe.
wrongs: A tour of nearby cafes with no mention of hazards.
The final performance review at the end of the placement.
A software tutorial unrelated to the site.
why: Health and safety induction is the opening briefing that tells a new person how to stay safe on that site.
example: On day one the intern is shown the fire exits, the assembly point, and how to report a spill.
scenario: It is day one and you do not know the fire exit or how to report a spill. Which briefing should you complete first?
scenarioAnswer: The health and safety induction
scenarioWrongs: A cafe tour
The end-of-placement review
A software tutorial with no site safety
scenarioWhy: Health and safety induction covers hazards, emergency routes, and reporting before other work.

definition: Anything at work with the potential to cause injury, ill health, or damage.
wrongs: The likelihood that harm will occur, which is part of risk rather than the source of harm.
A completed incident form.
A safe walkway with no source of harm.
why: A hazard is the source that could cause harm; risk also considers how likely and severe that harm is.
example: A trailing power cable across a walkway is reported as a hazard because someone could trip.
scenario: A power cable lies across a busy walkway and could trip someone. Which term names the cable in that state?
scenarioAnswer: A hazard
scenarioWrongs: A completed incident form
A clear walkway
The company's annual profit
scenarioWhy: A hazard is something that can cause harm, such as a cable that could trip a person.

definition: A systematic look at hazards, who could be harmed, how serious that harm could be, and what controls are needed.
wrongs: A guess that everything is fine because no one was hurt yesterday.
A list of hazards with no thought about controls.
The intern's personal reflection on a meeting.
why: A risk assessment examines hazards, people, severity, and controls rather than assuming past luck will continue.
example: Before interns enter the lab, the assessment lists chemicals, who is exposed, and the required gloves and ventilation.
scenario: Interns will enter a lab with chemicals. Which process should identify who could be harmed and which controls are required?
scenarioAnswer: A workplace risk assessment
scenarioWrongs: Assuming safety because yesterday was quiet
Listing chemicals and stopping there
A personal reflection on a meeting
scenarioWhy: A risk assessment examines hazards, who could be harmed, and the controls required.

definition: Equipment worn to reduce a remaining risk, such as gloves or eye protection, after other controls have been considered.
wrongs: The first and only control, used so the employer can ignore removing the hazard.
Ordinary fashion accessories with no safety function.
A software password.
why: Personal protective equipment reduces remaining risk to the wearer and does not replace removing the hazard where that is reasonable.
example: After spills cannot be fully removed, the lab requires goggles as well as keeping containers closed.
scenario: A lab still has a splash risk after containers are kept closed. Which extra control is personal protective equipment?
scenarioAnswer: Wearing goggles
scenarioWrongs: Ignoring the splash because goggles exist somewhere
A fashionable hat with no safety rating
A longer computer password
scenarioWhy: Goggles are equipment worn to reduce the remaining splash risk.

definition: An unplanned event that could have caused harm but did not, and that should still be reported so controls can improve.
wrongs: An injury that has already occurred.
A planned fire drill that goes as scripted.
A hazard that nobody has encountered yet.
why: A near miss is an event that nearly caused harm and is reported so the next occurrence can be prevented.
example: A box falls from a shelf and misses a colleague; the intern reports it even though nobody was hurt.
scenario: A box falls and misses a colleague, so nobody is hurt. Which action treats the event correctly?
scenarioAnswer: Report the near miss so the shelf can be fixed
scenarioWrongs: Ignore it because there was no injury
Record it as a completed fire drill
Wait until someone is actually injured
scenarioWhy: A near miss should be reported so controls improve before harm occurs.

definition: The agreed steps for raising the alarm, evacuating, and accounting for people when a serious incident occurs.
wrongs: The everyday process for making coffee.
A plan written after the evacuation and never practised.
A rule to finish the current email before leaving during a fire alarm.
why: An emergency procedure is the pre-agreed response, including alarm, evacuation, and accounting for people.
example: On the alarm, the intern stops work, uses the stairs, and reports to the assembly point named at induction.
scenario: The fire alarm sounds. Which sequence follows a typical emergency procedure?
scenarioAnswer: Leave by the stairs and go to the assembly point
scenarioWrongs: Finish the email first
Use the lift so you can carry the laptop
Stay to make coffee for the team
scenarioWhy: The emergency procedure is to evacuate by the safe route and account for people at the assembly point.

definition: The introduction to the site, team, tools, and daily routines that helps a new intern work safely and effectively.
wrongs: A technical exam given before the intern has seen the workplace.
The final reference written at the end.
A map of a different city.
why: Orientation introduces the newcomer to the actual workplace so they can start work safely.
example: The intern meets the team, learns where tools are stored, and is shown how the daily standup runs.
scenario: On the first morning you do not know the team, the tool store, or the standup time. Which activity should supply that?
scenarioAnswer: Workplace orientation
scenarioWrongs: A final reference
An exam before you see the site
A map of another city
scenarioWhy: Workplace orientation introduces the site, people, tools, and routines.

definition: An experienced colleague who offers informal guidance on how work is done, distinct from the supervisor who assigns and assesses tasks.
wrongs: The manager who sets official tasks and conducts the performance review.
A client who only receives the finished work.
A stranger met once at a conference.
why: A mentor advises informally; the supervisor remains the person who assigns and assesses official work.
example: A senior engineer explains how the team writes tickets, while the supervisor still assigns and signs off the work.
scenario: You want informal advice on how this team writes tickets, separate from the person who grades you. Which person fits?
scenarioAnswer: A mentor
scenarioWrongs: Only the manager who conducts the formal review
A client who receives the work
A stranger from a conference
scenarioWhy: A mentor gives informal guidance and is distinct from the supervisor who assigns and assesses.

definition: A running list of tasks undertaken, with dates and outcomes, used as evidence of what the intern actually did.
wrongs: A list of tasks the intern hopes to do but never starts.
The company's five-year strategy.
A log of only personal errands.
why: A task log records completed and current placement work so the intern can evidence what was done.
example: The log shows that on 3 May the intern documented three switches and sent the notes to the supervisor.
scenario: The tutor asks for evidence of the tasks you actually completed, with dates. Which record fits?
scenarioAnswer: A task log
scenarioWrongs: A wishlist of tasks never started
The five-year strategy
A log of personal errands
scenarioWhy: A task log lists work undertaken with dates and outcomes.

definition: A short regular summary for the supervisor of work completed, problems, and plans for the coming week.
wrongs: The full thesis written at the end of a degree.
A daily social-media story.
An annual company report to shareholders.
why: A weekly report keeps the supervisor informed of progress, problems, and the immediate plan.
example: On Friday the intern sends three completed tickets, one blocker, and the two tasks planned for Monday.
scenario: Your supervisor wants each Friday's completed work, blockers, and Monday's plan. Which document is that?
scenarioAnswer: A weekly report
scenarioWrongs: The final degree thesis
A social-media story
The shareholder annual report
scenarioWhy: A weekly report summarises completed work, problems, and the next week's plan.

definition: A curated set of evidence, such as work samples, reflections, and feedback, showing the learning objectives were met.
wrongs: A single timesheet with no work samples or reflection.
A folder of confidential client data taken home.
The host's marketing brochure.
why: A portfolio selects evidence that the intern met the learning objectives, without removing confidential material improperly.
example: The portfolio includes a redacted diagram, the supervisor's feedback, and a reflection on the switch-configuration goal.
scenario: The tutor wants proof you met the switch-configuration goal, without raw client data. Which set fits?
scenarioAnswer: A portfolio with a redacted sample, feedback, and a reflection
scenarioWrongs: Only a timesheet
A folder of confidential client files
The host's marketing brochure
scenarioWhy: An internship portfolio curates evidence of learning, such as samples, feedback, and reflection.

definition: A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound.
wrongs: A goal that says learn networking someday, with no measure or date.
A goal to become perfect at every technology by tomorrow.
A goal unrelated to the placement, such as learn to cook.
why: SMART is a test of whether a goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound.
example: Document ten live switches to the team template by 30 June is used instead of get better at networks.
scenario: Which placement goal is SMART?
scenarioAnswer: Document ten switches to the team template by 30 June
scenarioWrongs: Learn networking someday
Become perfect at every technology by tomorrow
Learn to cook during the placement
scenarioWhy: The switch goal is specific, measurable, realistic for the role, relevant, and dated.

definition: The difference between the skills a task or objective requires and the skills the intern can already demonstrate.
wrongs: A gap in the office fence.
The intern's age subtracted from the supervisor's age.
A missing page in a novel.
why: A skill gap is the missing capability between current skill and what the work requires.
example: The objective needs basic SQL, and the intern has never written a query, so that difference is the skill gap.
scenario: The role needs basic SQL and you have never written a query. Which description fits that difference?
scenarioAnswer: A skill gap
scenarioWrongs: A hole in the office fence
The age difference with the supervisor
A missing page in a novel
scenarioWhy: The difference between required SQL skill and current skill is a skill gap.

definition: The limit that keeps relationships and requests appropriate to the intern role, including refusing work they are not authorised to do.
wrongs: A rule that interns must do any personal favour a colleague requests.
A requirement to share personal problems with every client.
Permission to approve expenditure the intern was told not to approve.
why: Professional boundaries keep the intern's relationships and decisions inside the authority of the role.
example: A client asks the intern to approve a discount; the intern declines and refers the request to the supervisor.
scenario: A client asks you to approve a discount you were told only a manager may approve. Which response respects the professional boundary?
scenarioAnswer: Decline and refer the request to the supervisor
scenarioWrongs: Approve it to seem helpful
Share your personal finances with the client while deciding
Ask the client to keep the approval secret
scenarioWhy: The boundary of the role excludes approving a discount, so the intern must refer it.

definition: Seeking guidance early when a task is unclear or beyond current skill, rather than guessing on work that affects others.
wrongs: Hiding confusion until a client is given a wrong answer.
Handing the entire role to someone else on day one.
Asking the same answered question every hour without trying the advice.
why: Asking for help at the right time prevents harmful guesses while the intern still attempts the work they can do.
example: Unsure which VLAN a port should use, the intern asks the supervisor before changing the live switch.
scenario: You are unsure which VLAN a live switch port should use. Which action is the right request for help?
scenarioAnswer: Ask the supervisor before changing the live port
scenarioWrongs: Guess on the live switch and tell nobody
Give the whole placement back on day one
Wait until a client outage proves the guess was wrong
scenarioWhy: Asking before changing live equipment avoids a harmful guess on work beyond current certainty.

definition: Expected behaviour in meetings, including arriving prepared, letting others speak, and leaving with clear actions.
wrongs: Arriving late, interrupting, and leaving with no note of actions.
Reading unrelated messages for the whole meeting.
Speaking only in jokes that hide the decision.
why: Meeting etiquette helps the group reach and record decisions without excluding people.
example: The intern reads the agenda, speaks when invited, and repeats the action they own before leaving.
scenario: You are invited to a client meeting with an agenda. Which behaviour matches meeting etiquette?
scenarioAnswer: Read the agenda, take your turn, and confirm your action
scenarioWrongs: Arrive late and interrupt
Read unrelated messages throughout
Hide the decision inside jokes
scenarioWhy: Meeting etiquette means being prepared, sharing the floor, and leaving with clear actions.

definition: Paying full attention, checking that you have understood, and responding to what was actually said.
wrongs: Waiting silently for a turn to repeat your own point, without checking theirs.
Typing an unrelated message while they speak.
Agreeing immediately to a request you did not hear.
why: Active listening checks understanding of the other person's message before you respond.
example: The intern restates the client's fault symptoms and asks whether that summary is right before suggesting a fix.
scenario: A client describes a fault. Which response shows active listening?
scenarioAnswer: Restate the symptoms and ask if that summary is right
scenarioWrongs: Wait only to repeat your own idea
Type an unrelated message while they speak
Agree to a fix you did not hear
scenarioWhy: Active listening checks that you understood what was said before you act on it.

definition: Recording decisions, facts, and actions during a meeting or task so they can be confirmed and followed up.
wrongs: Trying to remember every action with no written note.
Recording a client's secrets in a public notebook you leave behind.
Writing only doodles with no decisions.
why: Notes capture decisions and actions so they can be checked and done, while still respecting confidentiality.
example: During the standup the intern writes the two actions, the owners, and the deadlines, then confirms them.
scenario: The standup assigns you two actions with deadlines. Which note-taking practice is sound?
scenarioAnswer: Write the actions, owners, and deadlines, then confirm them
scenarioWrongs: Rely on memory alone
Leave a public notebook of client secrets behind
Doodle and record no actions
scenarioWhy: Useful notes record the decisions and actions so they can be confirmed and followed up.

definition: An agreement to finish a task by a stated time, accepted only when that time is realistic.
wrongs: Saying yes to every date to appear keen, including dates you know you will miss.
Ignoring a date you already accepted.
Moving a date secretly without telling the person who is waiting.
why: A deadline commitment should be realistic and, once made, should be kept or renegotiated early.
example: Asked for a report by tomorrow morning, the intern explains that testing finishes at noon and offers end of day instead.
scenario: You are asked for a report tomorrow morning, but testing cannot finish until noon. Which response is a sound deadline commitment?
scenarioAnswer: Offer a realistic end-of-day delivery and agree that
scenarioWrongs: Promise tomorrow morning knowing you will miss it
Accept the morning and then ignore it
Slip the date secretly
scenarioWhy: A deadline should be agreed only when it is realistic, and then honoured.

definition: The decisions and actions an intern is allowed to take without further approval.
wrongs: Every decision a permanent manager is allowed to take.
No decisions at all, even those the supervisor has explicitly delegated.
Whatever a client demands in the moment.
why: Scope of authority is the set of actions already delegated to the intern; other actions need approval.
example: The intern may close low-priority tickets but must ask before rebooting a production server.
scenario: You may close low-priority tickets, but a reboot of production was not delegated. Which action stays inside your authority?
scenarioAnswer: Close the low-priority ticket
scenarioWrongs: Reboot production because a client asked
Approve a budget change
Sign a contract for the company
scenarioWhy: Scope of authority includes only the actions delegated to the intern, such as closing low-priority tickets.

definition: Telling the supervisor about a problem the intern cannot safely or properly resolve alone.
wrongs: Posting the problem on a public network before telling the supervisor.
Hiding a safety problem to avoid looking inexperienced.
Asking an uninvolved friend to change company systems.
why: Escalation at work takes an unresolved or unsafe problem to the person who can act.
example: When a client demands a production change, the intern stops and tells the supervisor rather than making the change.
scenario: A client demands a production change you are not allowed to make. Which step is proper workplace escalation?
scenarioAnswer: Tell the supervisor and wait for a decision
scenarioWrongs: Make the change so the client is happy
Post the argument publicly first
Ask a friend outside the company to log in and do it
scenarioWhy: Escalation means taking a problem you cannot properly resolve to the supervisor who can.

definition: A difference about tasks or behaviour that should be raised early, calmly, and with the person who can resolve it.
wrongs: A reason to insult a colleague in a public channel.
Something an intern must always ignore, even when work is blocked.
A licence to refuse every task you dislike.
why: A workplace disagreement should be addressed early and through the proper person, without public insult.
example: Two interns disagree about who owns a ticket, so they ask the supervisor rather than arguing in the client chat.
scenario: You and another intern disagree about who owns a ticket, and the client chat is not the place to argue. Which step fits?
scenarioAnswer: Ask the supervisor to decide ownership calmly
scenarioWrongs: Insult the other intern in the client chat
Ignore the block until the deadline fails
Refuse all further tasks
scenarioWhy: A disagreement about task ownership should be raised calmly with the person who can resolve it.

definition: The shared expectations a team sets for how members communicate, share work, and treat one another.
wrongs: A national law that applies whether or not the team discussed it.
One person's private habit that the team has not agreed.
The default settings of a chat tool, if the team works differently.
why: Team norms are the expectations the team itself agrees, such as how quickly messages are answered.
example: The team agrees that questions in the project channel get a reply the same working day.
scenario: The team has agreed that project-channel questions get a same-day reply. Which idea is that agreement?
scenarioAnswer: A team norm
scenarioWrongs: A private habit nobody else accepted
A software default the team does not follow
A law the team never discussed
scenarioWhy: A shared expectation about how the team communicates is a team norm.

definition: Hearing comments without immediate defensiveness, checking what is expected, and applying the agreed change.
wrongs: Arguing before you have understood the comment.
Agreeing aloud and then repeating the same error with no attempt to change.
Taking the comment as a judgement of your worth as a person.
why: Receiving feedback well means understanding the expected change and then applying it.
example: Told the labels are too small, the intern asks which size the client needs and updates the diagram that day.
scenario: Your supervisor says the diagram labels are too small for the client. Which response receives that feedback well?
scenarioAnswer: Confirm the size required and update the diagram
scenarioWrongs: Argue before asking what size is needed
Agree and submit the same labels again
Treat the comment as an attack on your worth
scenarioWhy: Receiving feedback means clarifying the expected change and applying it.

definition: The intern's own judgement of progress against the learning objectives, supported by examples from the work.
wrongs: The supervisor's mark, which is someone else's judgement.
A claim of excellence with no example from the placement.
A copy of a classmate's assessment.
why: Self-assessment is the intern's evidence-based judgement of their own progress toward the agreed objectives.
example: The intern writes that the switch goal is partly met, citing four documented switches out of the ten aimed for.
scenario: You must judge your own progress on the switch goal using placement evidence. Which statement is self-assessment?
scenarioAnswer: Four of the ten switches are documented, so the goal is partly met
scenarioWrongs: The supervisor's mark alone
A claim of excellence with no example
A classmate's assessment copied over
scenarioWhy: Self-assessment uses your own examples to judge progress against the objective.

definition: The end-of-placement document that describes duties, evidence of learning, and reflection against the agreed objectives.
wrongs: A one-line timesheet total.
The host's sales brochure.
A daily standup note from week one only.
why: The final report pulls duties, evidence, and reflection together against the objectives agreed at the start.
example: The report describes the network tasks, shows the checklist evidence, and reflects on the configuration objective.
scenario: The faculty wants one end document covering duties, evidence, and reflection on the agreed goals. Which document is that?
scenarioAnswer: The final internship report
scenarioWrongs: A one-line hours total
The host's sales brochure
Only the first standup note
scenarioWhy: The final internship report brings together duties, learning evidence, and reflection.

definition: A brief document that tells the next person the status of unfinished work, where files are, and what still needs attention.
wrongs: A goodbye card with no work status.
A deleted folder and no explanation.
A full rewrite of the company strategy.
why: A handover note lets the next person continue unfinished work without guessing where things stand.
example: On the last day the intern leaves a note listing two open tickets, the file paths, and the test still to run.
scenario: You are leaving with two tickets still open. Which document lets the next person continue them?
scenarioAnswer: A handover note with status, file paths, and the remaining test
scenarioWrongs: A goodbye card with no status
Deleting the folder without explanation
Rewriting the company strategy
scenarioWhy: A handover note states unfinished work, where the files are, and what still needs attention.

definition: A statement from a supervisor about the intern's observed conduct and performance, given truthfully and usually with the intern's knowledge.
wrongs: A reference the intern writes and signs as if they were the supervisor.
A promise to hide poor attendance if asked.
A social-media like from a classmate.
why: A professional reference is the supervisor's truthful account of observed work, not a self-written endorsement.
example: The supervisor agrees to describe the intern's punctuality and the switches they documented, and will not invent extra duties.
scenario: A future employer asks your supervisor about your placement. Which reference is professional?
scenarioAnswer: A truthful account of conduct and work the supervisor observed
scenarioWrongs: A reference you write and sign as the supervisor
A promise to hide poor attendance
A classmate's social-media reaction
scenarioWhy: A professional reference is the supervisor's truthful statement about observed conduct and performance.
